 A.4 Chapter 4

Conceptual exercises
Solution 4.1. 1. A bound state refers to a quantum state in which a parti­
cle is co­fined to a finite region of space by a potential well, resulting in
discrete energy levels. An unbound state, on the other hand, refers to a
state where the particle is not co­fined in the potential well, leading to a
continuum of energy levels.
2. The key difference in the energy spectra is that bound states have quan­
tized energy levels within the potential well, while unbound states have
a continuous energy spectrum, allowing the particle to have any energy
above a certain threshold.

Solution 4.3. Quantum tunneling is the phenomenon where a particle has
a finite probability of crossing a potential barrier, even if its energy is less
than the height of the barrier. This occurs because, according to quantum
mechanics, particles exhibit wave-like properties and their wave functions
can penetrate through barriers.

Solution 5.11. The boundary condition for φ implies m = 0, ±1, ±2, · · ·
(see Eq. (5.17)), while Eq. (5.23) imposes −l ≤ m ≤ +l . Note the order of the
derivative in Eq. (5.23): l + m. The smallest possible order is zero, hence
mmin = −l . Also note that the function to be differentiated l + m times,
i.e., (x 2 − 1)l , is a polynomial of maximum order x 2l , and thus 2l is the
maximum number of derivatives before Plm (x ) becomes zero. Therefore,
l + mmax = 2l , implying mmax = +l . These simple calculations lead to the
final result: −l ≤ m ≤ +l .

 A.6 Chapter 6

Conceptual exercises
Solution 6.1. This commutation relation highlights that it is impossible to
precisely determine two components of angular momentum at the same
time. Measuring one component causes the other two to become uncer­
tain -- a consequence of the uncertainty principle. Mathematically, when
these components are represented as matrices, they cannot be diagonal­
ized at once. A basis that diagonalizes one component ensures the other
two remain non-diagonal.

Solution 6.2. The variance represents the dispersion of a given distribu­
tion. Considering the commutation relation of angular momentum, it is
not possible to know all three components simultaneously; that is, if we

22 Solutions to the exercises

measure the value of one of them (say, the z component), we lose in­
formation about the other two components (this effect is related to the
uncertainty principle). For this reason, the variance of the z component of
angular momentum is zero, meaning we are certain of its value because it
has been measured. In other words, there is no distribution of eigenvalues
of angular momentum for this component. The opposite situation occurs
for the other two components of angular momentum. Once the z compo­
nent has been measured, the other two components cannot be determined
exactly. We know the variance of these two components (see the standard
deviation in Eq. (6.69))....

Solution 7.1. One reason to expand the Hilbert space is to enable math­
ematical operations involving matrices that represent operators of differ­
ent dimensions. For example, consider the Hamiltonian Ĥ = Ŝz2 (where

Solutions to the exercises 33

Ŝz = Ŝ1z + Ŝ2z ), for s1 = 1/2 and s2 = 1. How to add a 2 × 2 matrix to an­
other 3 × 3? Only if we expand the Hilbert space such that both matrices
have the same dimension 6 × 6.

Solution 7.2. The first Hund’s rule d­fines in which orbitals to place
electrons of a multi-electron atom. Due to the Coulombian repulsion, we
cannot place two electrons in the same orbital when other orbitals are
available. This rule maximizes the value of the effective atomic spin. The
second Hund’s rule, on the other hand, maximizes the value of orbital an­
gular momentum. Let’s consider a Bohr atom, for instance. If two electrons
are orbiting this nucleus, Coulombian repulsion is minimized if their or­
bits are in the same direction....
